cards.explanation: The answer is the Pharisees. They say to Jesus, “Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” (Mark 2:24). The disciples are just picking grain, and somebody still has a question about it. I'd have pretended to admire the scenery and kept moving, friends, because I fold fast when people stare.

The answer is the consecrated bread. Jesus says David “…entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread…” (Mark 2:26). David was Israel's king later on (2 Samuel 5:3), but here he's just a hungry man. Jesus names Abiathar as high priest at the time, so He's pointing at a real moment from Israel's story. Hungry people and bread, friends. I understand that one on a deep level.

The answer is True. Jesus says the consecrated bread “…was lawful only for the priests.” (Mark 2:26). So David ate something that was set aside for the priests. That's the very thing Jesus holds up when the Pharisees bring up what's lawful. He's pointing at what was done, and He doesn't hide that it was only for priests.

The answer is that the Sabbath was made for man. Jesus declares, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). He says it right after the story about David. Think of an oven mitt, friends: it was made for my hands, not my hands for the mitt.

The answer is False. Jesus says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:27). That "not" settles it. He says the Sabbath was made for man, and He says man wasn't made for the Sabbath. Small word, big difference.

The answer is Lord. Jesus says, “Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” (Mark 2:28). He's talking about Himself with that name. Lord means He has authority over it, even over the Sabbath the Pharisees just asked about. Straight answer, no hedging, and I admire that, friends, because I hedge about a burnt batch for ten minutes.

The answer is that they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath. Mark 3:2 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” A man with a withered hand is right there, and they're watching Jesus to see what He will do. I think that has to feel like standing under a very bright oven light.

The answer is True. Mark 3:2 says, “In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.” The text gives their reason right there. They were watching in order to accuse Him. That's a heavy reason to have your eyes on someone.

The answer is that they stay silent. Mark 3:4 says, “But they were silent.” Jesus asks a question about doing good or evil, saving life or destroying it, and nobody says a word. I've been in that quiet room before, friends, usually right after I ask who ate the last cookie.

The answer is restored. Mark 3:5 says Jesus told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” Then it says, “So he stretched it out, and it was restored.” The man did what he was told, and his hand was whole. I love that one, friends. My own edges took a miracle to fix, so I know a good restoration when I see one.

The answer is the Herodians. Mark 3:6 says the Pharisees “…went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.” They leave right after the man's hand is restored. This is a heavy moment, and I think it's okay to say that out loud. The text names the Herodians, so that's who we name.

The answer is kill. That's the word in Mark 3:6: they began plotting “…how they might kill Jesus.” A hand was restored, and right after it the plotting begins. The next time you read this story, friends, notice how fast things turn in just one verse.
